segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey, to be ready for every good work,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to slander no one, not to pick fights, to be considerate, showing all gentleness to all people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we too were once senseless, disobedient, led astray, enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures, spending our lives in malice and envy, detestable, hating one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for humanity appeared,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: it was not because of works we ourselves had done in righteousness but in keeping with his mercy that he saved us, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may take care to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and useful to people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But keep clear of foolish debates, genealogies, quarrels, and fights over the law, for they are useless and empty.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a divisive person,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that such a person is warped and goes on sinning, self-condemned.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Make every effort to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, so that they lack nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And let our own people also learn to devote themselves to good works to meet pressing needs, so that they will not be unfruitful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with all of you.

notes.note: The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a considerate, unassertive way of treating others, and 'gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

The Greek word, philanthrōpia, was a stock term for the generosity expected of gods, kings and public benefactors toward those in their care. Together with 'appeared' and 'Savior', it is language a first-century reader would recognise from the public praise of rulers, here applied to God.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: 'righteousness' here and 'justified' in verse 7 share a root, as do 'righteous' and 'just'. The contrast is deliberate: it was not our own right conduct that saved us, but God's grace that set us right.

notes.phrase: the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit
notes.traditional: the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost
notes.note: The Greek can mean one washing that brings both rebirth and renewal, the Spirit being the agent of both, or two things: a washing of rebirth, and a renewal by the Spirit. The rendering leaves this open, as the Greek does. Most interpreters take the 'washing' to refer to baptism, though some understand it as a figure for inner cleansing.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer 'life of the age to come'.

This translation normally renders the adjective 'faithful' or 'believing', but in current English a saying is not called faithful. The sense here is that the statement can be relied on, so 'trustworthy' is used. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and here most likely points back to the summary in verses 4 to 7.

notes.traditional: be careful to maintain good works
notes.note: The verb can mean to take the lead in something, to busy oneself with it, or to practise a trade. Most translations take it as applying oneself to good deeds. A minority reading is 'engage in honourable occupations', which would also fit verse 14 with its mention of meeting needs.

notes.traditional: a man that is an heretic
notes.note: The Greek word is the source of the English 'heretic', but in this period it described someone who forms a faction or causes division, not someone who holds a formally condemned doctrine. That later sense developed in the following centuries. Most modern translations likewise have 'divisive' or 'factious'.

Several cities bore this name, which means 'victory city'. The one meant is usually thought to be Nicopolis in Epirus, on the west coast of Greece, a port where a traveller could wait out the winter when sea voyages stopped.

The word means an expert in law. In the Gospels it refers to experts in the Jewish law, and the same adjective is used in verse 9 of disputes 'over the law'. Since Zenas has a Greek name, he may have been a jurist in Roman or Greek law, and the text does not settle which.

The verb means more than saying goodbye. It was the usual term for equipping travellers with food, money and whatever else they needed for the next stage of a journey, which is why the sentence continues 'so that they lack nothing'.
The letter is addressed to Titus alone, but the closing 'you' is plural. The blessing reaches past him to the congregations in Crete, who were evidently expected to hear the letter read.

candidates.reason: The word covers both abusive speech against people ('slander') and against God ('blaspheme'), and translators split unpredictably between the two across the New Testament.

It recurs in virtue lists (Philippians 4:5; 1 Timothy 3:3; James 3:17; 1 Peter 2:18) and is variously rendered gentle, forbearing, reasonable and considerate, which collides with the register's 'gentle' for πραΰς.
It is common across the letters and rendered variously as lust, desire, passion and craving; 'lust' wrongly narrows it to sexual desire for modern readers.
It is used in the Gospels for experts in the Jewish law and here possibly for a secular jurist, so the choice between 'lawyer' and 'expert in the law' needs a single policy.
Its range runs from lead and manage (Romans 12:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:12; 1 Timothy 3:4–5, 5:17) to care for and engage in, and the choice affects how church leadership passages read.
